passage:
Tuesday: Maria's phone buzzed with a party invite from classmates. She typed "yes", then deleted it. Mum's voice was in her head: aunties and neighbours notice which friends a girl is seen with and what she wears. Maria told Mum she was staying late for extra maths.
Friday: Her mother Sarita met the maths teacher in the market, who said there was no extra class. That night the kitchen was silent. "I didn't want you to think badly of me," Maria said to the floor, "or the neighbours to talk about us."
Sunday: Sarita put two cups of tea on the table. "Tell me about these friends. What do you like about them? Let's decide what matters together, not by what the neighbours think." Maria's shoulders loosened, and she found the group photo on her phone.

qa.q: What excuse did Maria give Mum for not going to the party?
qa.a: She said she was staying late for extra maths.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when she deleted her 'yes' and told Mum about extra maths?
qa.a: She felt anxious and afraid of being judged, since she believed neighbours would notice her friends and clothes and that it would reflect on the family.

qa.q: What turning point on Sunday made it easier for Maria to tell the truth?
qa.a: Sarita asked about the friends with curiosity and offered to decide together what matters, not by what neighbours think, so Maria did not have to hide.

qa.q: How might Sarita have felt when she learned there was no extra maths class?
qa.a: Sarita was probably hurt and worried, shown by the silent kitchen, but she chose to talk with Maria on Sunday instead of scolding.

grounding: A teenager girl feels her friendships and choices carry the family's reputation, lies, and trust grows when a parent discusses values.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage: My name is Mohit, and I want to tell you about Lalremsiami, who lived next door to us in Shillong when we were both sixteen. She loved a small music group at college but told her parents she was at the library. Her father was a respected man, and she felt every friend and every dress was being weighed against the family name. So she lied, a little more each month, and grew quiet at home. One evening her mother found guitar picks in her bag. Lalremsiami waited for shouting. Instead her mother asked, "What do you love about it? And what were you afraid we would say?" Lalremsiami cried and told everything. The next week her parents met the group's teacher. After that she never needed the library story.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami tell her parents she was when she went to the music group?
qa.a: She told them she was at the library.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she kept lying month after month?
qa.a: She was anxious and weighed down, feeling watched for the family name, which made her grow quiet at home.

qa.q: What choice by Lalremsiami's mother changed the situation?
qa.a: When she found the guitar picks, her mother asked what Lalremsiami loved and what she feared instead of shouting, and that honest question led to the truth.

qa.q: Why might Lalremsiami's mother have asked what she was afraid they would say?
qa.a: She probably saw that the lies came from fear, not from wanting to deceive, and wanted to earn her daughter's honesty.

grounding: A teenager feels friends and clothes carry family reputation, lies out of fear, and a family that talks values earns trust.

"Aditi, you're not wearing jeans to Mehr's party. What will the Kulkarnis think if they see you?"
"Mumma, it's a birthday party. Everyone wears jeans."
"Everyone isn't my daughter. Our family has a name in this building."
"So my clothes are the family's name?"
"Don't argue. Wear the salwar."
"...Last month I told you I was at Nupur's house. I was at the mall with the whole group. I lied because I knew you'd say no."
Silence.
"You lied to me?"
"Because every time, it's about what people will think. Never about what I think, or whether it's actually safe."
Sarika sat down slowly. "...Okay. Tell me, then. Who's going? Where is it? When will you be home?"
"Six girls, her flat, back by nine. Her mother will be there."
"Then go. In jeans. And no more lies, Aditi. If we talk, I'll try to listen."

qa.q: What time did Aditi say she would be back?
qa.a: Aditi said, "Six girls, her flat, back by nine."

qa.q: How was Sarika feeling when she sat down slowly?
qa.a: Sarika felt shocked and hurt to learn about the lie, and also thoughtful, realising her focus on appearances had pushed Aditi to hide things.

qa.q: What made the conversation turn?
qa.a: Aditi admitted her lie and explained why, and Sarika shifted from what people think to real questions about safety, which built trust.

qa.q: How does Aditi seem to feel about carrying the family's name in her clothes?
qa.a: Aditi feels stifled and frustrated, as if her own thoughts don't matter, which led her to lie.

grounding: A teenage girl feels her clothes carry her family's reputation, which led her to lie, and a talk about values and safety begins to rebuild trust.

passage:
Two years ago, when I was fifteen, I started lying to my parents almost every day. I'm Alka, and I'm not proud of it.
It began with the study group. Four of us, two boys and two girls, met at the library. Papa said, "People will talk. A girl from our family with boys?" My brother Jatin went to cricket camp with anyone he liked, and nobody said a word.
So I told them it was only girls. Then about the school trip. Each lie made me feel smaller.
One evening Jatin caught me in a lie. He didn't tell. Instead he said to Papa, at dinner, "Why do you trust me and not Alka? She's the one with better marks."
Papa was quiet for a long time. Later he asked me who was in my study group. I told him the truth. He said, "Next time, just tell me." It wasn't perfect. But I stopped lying.

qa.q: Who went to cricket camp with anyone he liked?
qa.a: Alka's brother Jatin went to cricket camp with anyone he liked.

qa.q: How did each lie make Alka feel?
qa.a: Each lie made Alka feel smaller, ashamed and trapped by the double rule.

qa.q: What could families like Alka's learn from this story?
qa.a: Talking about values and trust, rather than watching what people will say, makes it easier for a teenager to be honest.

qa.q: Why might Jatin react differently from Papa?
qa.a: Jatin saw the unfairness of different rules for him and Alka, so he stood up for his sister instead of worrying about talk.

grounding: A teenage girl feels her friendships carry the family's reputation, which leads her to lie, until a fairer conversation earns her honesty.

School counsellor's note, Thursday.
Zeenat, 15, was referred by her class teacher after missing three debate practices while telling her family she was attending them. Her friend Indu came with her.
Zeenat told me, very quietly, that her father doesn't allow her to stay after school because "people might see her with boys and talk." She loves debating and wanted to practise. So she said she was at practice, but went to Indu's house nearby, where Indu's mother helped them prepare. Then she felt terrible and stopped going altogether.
She said, "I'm tired of lying. But the truth is always no."
I told her that her wish was reasonable and that the lying was a sign of pressure, not a bad character.
Next step: with her permission, I called her mother the same afternoon and invited both parents to meet the debate coach, see where practice happens and who supervises it.

qa.q: Where did Zeenat actually go instead of practice?
qa.a: She went to Indu's house nearby, where Indu's mother helped them prepare.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when she said "I'm tired of lying"?
qa.a: Zeenat felt exhausted and guilty, trapped between her love of debating and her father's fear of what people would say.

qa.q: Why was inviting the parents to meet the debate coach a wise step?
qa.a: It moves the conversation from appearances to real facts, like who supervises practice, which can help the family trust Zeenat.

qa.q: How might Indu feel about being part of the lie?
qa.a: Indu may feel uneasy and protective, wanting to help her friend but aware that the secret was weighing on Zeenat.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenage girl whose family's fear of talk leads her to lie, and a step toward discussing real values and safety.

subtopic: Honour and shame vs guilt cultures
passage:
Jaya's diary, Saturday night.
Wore the jeans to Swati's birthday. Took the salwar in my bag and changed in her bathroom before coming home, like always. Mummy smiled at the salwar. I felt sick.
It isn't even about jeans. It's that my cousin Rahul goes anywhere in shorts and nobody says "what will the Guptas think". When I laughed too loud at the bus stop last week, Chachi told Mummy before I even got home: "A grown girl, laughing like that in public!"
Tonight Swati's mother dropped me back and said, "Jaya was the one who stayed to clean up." Mummy looked at the bag in my hand. She knew. I waited for the shouting.
Instead she said, "Why do you feel you have to hide from me?" We talked till midnight. I told her about the jeans. She told me about her own mother. We didn't fix it. But we talked about what matters, not what the Guptas see.

qa.q: Where did Jaya change back into the salwar?
qa.a: She changed in Swati's bathroom before coming home.

qa.q: What did Jaya feel when Mummy smiled at the salwar?
qa.a: Jaya felt sick with guilt about hiding the jeans and pretending.

qa.q: What made the midnight talk different from the usual pattern?
qa.a: Mummy asked why Jaya felt the need to hide instead of shouting, so they could discuss values rather than appearances, which builds trust.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when she saw the bag and understood?
qa.a: Mummy likely felt hurt and surprised that Jaya had been hiding, but cared enough about their trust to ask gently instead of scolding.

grounding: It illustrates a teenage girl who feels her clothes and choices carry the family's reputation, which pushes her into hiding, and a parent who turns the talk to values.
